chapter_summary:
In Scrum, clarity and transparency are paramount. This is achieved through the use of three primary artifacts: the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog, and the Increment. These artifacts represent work or value, providing transparency and opportunities for inspection and adaptation. They are designed to maximize transparency of key information so that everybody has the same understanding of the artifact.

Let's start with the **Product Backlog**. This is the single, authoritative source of work to be done on the product. It's an ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product and is maintained by the Product Owner. The Product Backlog is dynamic; it's never complete and evolves as the product and the environment in which it will be used evolves. Items in the Product Backlog are typically described as user stories, features, or epics, and are ordered by value, risk, necessity, and dependencies. A well-managed Product Backlog exhibits the characteristics of DEEP: **D**etailed appropriately (higher priority items are more detailed), **E**stimated (effort is estimated), **E**mergent (constantly updated and refined), and **P**rioritized (ordered by the Product Owner). A common mistake is allowing the Product Backlog to become stale, unrefined, or filled with items that lack clarity or value. Without ongoing refinement, the Product Backlog becomes a bottleneck for Sprint Planning and can lead to a Development Team working on features that don't deliver maximum value. The Product Owner works continuously with the Development Team and stakeholders to refine the Product Backlog, ensuring items are ready for future Sprints.

Next, we have the **Sprint Backlog**. This artifact is a subset of the Product Backlog items selected for the current Sprint, plus the plan for delivering them and realizing the Sprint Goal. It's the Development Team's forecast of functionality that will be in the next Increment and the work needed to deliver that functionality. The Sprint Backlog is owned solely by the Development Team. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Development Team plans to accomplish during the Sprint. As the Sprint progresses, the Development Team inspects its progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapts the Sprint Backlog as needed. This flexibility allows the team to learn and adjust, rather than rigidly adhering to an outdated plan. A common mistake is treating the Sprint Backlog as a fixed contract, where no changes are allowed once Sprint Planning is over. While the Sprint Goal should remain stable, the Development Team can and should update the Sprint Backlog as they gain new insights or face unexpected challenges, always with the Sprint Goal in mind.

Finally, we come to the **Increment**. This is the sum of all the Product Backlog items completed during a Sprint and the value of the increments of all previous Sprints. At the end of each Sprint, a "Done" Increment must be available. It must be in a usable condition regardless of whether the Product Owner decides to actually release it. The Increment is a concrete step toward the Product Goal. For an Increment to be "Done," it must adhere to the **Definition of Done (DoD)**. The DoD is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product. It creates transparency by providing a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment. If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released, nor can it even be presented at the Sprint Review. It simply reverts to the Product Backlog. A critical mistake is having a weak or non-existent Definition of Done, leading to "almost Done" work, accumulating technical debt, and a lack of true transparency about the product's actual state. The DoD ensures quality and consistency across Sprints and is a commitment by the Development Team.

Consider a real-world example: building an online food ordering system. The Product Backlog might contain items like "As a customer, I want to view restaurant menus," "As a restaurant, I want to receive orders," and "As a customer, I want to pay securely." For a given Sprint, the Sprint Backlog might include "Develop menu display page," "Implement 'add to cart' functionality," and "Write unit tests for checkout process." The Increment at the end of the Sprint would be a functional, tested piece of the application (e.g., a working menu display with add-to-cart, even if checkout isn't fully integrated) that adheres to the Definition of Done (e.g., code reviewed, tested, deployed to staging). These artifacts work in concert, providing the necessary transparency and points of inspection for the Scrum Team and stakeholders to make informed decisions and continuously adapt to deliver the most valuable product possible.

screens.title: Scrum Artifacts: Transparency and Progress
screens.subtitle: How Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment make work visible and usable

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on the three Scrum artifacts that make product work transparent and inspectable. You'll learn what the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment are, who owns them, and how they relate to the Definition of Done. We will use concrete examples — like an online food ordering system and a smart home hub — to show how items move from a long-term, evolving backlog into a focused Sprint plan and then into a usable increment. Understanding these artifacts matters because they are the primary signals a Scrum Team uses to make decisions, avoid technical debt, and deliver value consistently. We will also highlight common mistakes, such as stale backlog items or treating a Sprint Backlog as an unchangeable contract. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain DEEP qualities for the Product Backlog, describe how the Sprint Backlog supports adaptation toward a Sprint Goal, and explain why a solid Definition of Done prevents “almost done” work from hiding real progress. Consider, as we move forward, one reflective question: when was the last time a backlog item you relied on lacked enough detail to plan a Sprint?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Artifacts create shared, inspectable information: Product Backlog for what might be built, Sprint Backlog for what will be built in the Sprint, and Increment for what is actually Done.

narration.text: These applied objectives guide you toward concrete behaviors the team can adopt. You will practice backlog refinement so high-priority items are sufficiently detailed and estimated before Sprint Planning. You will learn to treat the Sprint Backlog as a flexible, team-owned forecast that changes when new learning emerges during the Sprint. You will use the Definition of Done as an objective quality gate so incomplete work never masquerades as finished. Finally, you will diagnose common mistakes — stale backlogs, weak DoD, and rigid Sprint Backlogs — and adopt small fixes to avoid them. For example, allocating a modest portion of team capacity for regular refinement prevents ambiguous items from derailing planning. These skills help a team make faster, safer decisions and maintain a consistent cadence of valuable increments. As you practice, note one habit you can change immediately to increase transparency in your next Sprint.

screens.title: The three Scrum artifacts
screens.subtitle: What each artifact represents and the shared goal of transparency

narration.text: Scrum uses three artifacts to represent work and value: the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog, and the Increment. Each artifact is a transparent container of information so the Scrum Team and stakeholders have the same shared understanding. The Product Backlog is the single source of requirements for product changes; it lists, orders, and evolves potential work items as the product and context change. The Sprint Backlog is a subset of that work selected for a Sprint, together with a plan for achieving the Sprint Goal; it is owned by the Development Team and is a real-time view of work in progress. The Increment is the sum of completed Product Backlog items this Sprint and all prior Sprints, and it must meet the Definition of Done to be considered releasable. A common misconception is to think artifacts are static documents. In reality they are living information radiators: the Product Backlog is emergent, the Sprint Backlog is adaptable during the Sprint, and the Increment grows with each Done piece. As an example, imagine an online food ordering product: the Product Backlog contains features like menu browsing and secure payment; the Sprint Backlog picks the next set of features and tasks to deliver a working menu display; the Increment is that working display tested and ready for staging. Takeaway: artifacts are how Scrum makes intentions and progress visible so teams can inspect and adapt effectively.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Artifacts are living sources of truth: backlog items represent potential work, sprint backlogs represent near-term plans, and increments represent done value.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Core Concept

The three artifacts

Artifacts provide a shared, inspectable representation of work and progress, enabling adaptation.

Product Backlog
Single, ordered source of everything needed for the product. Emergent and owned by the Product Owner.
Sprint Backlog
Team-owned plan plus selected Product Backlog items for the Sprint. Adapted as the team learns.
Increment
Sum of Done Product Backlog items that meet the Definition of Done — usable and potentially releasable.
Example: Online Food Ordering
Product Backlog: view menus, secure payment, order history. Sprint Backlog: build menu display and add-to-cart this Sprint. Increment: tested menu display ready for staging that meets DoD.
Common Mistake
Treating artifacts as static documents leads to outdated plans and poor decisions.
Key Takeaway

Artifacts are the team's shared information radiators: keep them current to enable inspection and adaptation.

screens.title: Product Backlog and DEEP
screens.subtitle: What DEEP means and why it prevents planning bottlenecks

narration.text: The Product Backlog is the authoritative list of everything that might be needed in the product, and its quality determines how well a Scrum Team plans and delivers. DEEP is an acronym that captures four essential characteristics: Detailed appropriately, Estimated, Emergent, and Prioritized. Detailed appropriately means that higher-priority items have more detail so they are ready for near-term planning, while lower-priority items can remain coarse. Estimated ensures the team understands relative size or effort so they can forecast, while Emergent acknowledges the backlog constantly changes as new learning and feedback arrive. Prioritized means the Product Owner orders work by value, risk, and necessity so the most important items surface first. A common mistake is allowing the backlog to become stale or filled with vague items; this creates a bottleneck for Sprint Planning because teams waste time clarifying goals instead of building. For example, in the online food ordering product, a top-priority story like "view menus" should include acceptance criteria and rough estimates, while a far-future idea like "loyalty program" can stay high-level. Practically, schedule regular refinement sessions consuming a modest portion of capacity, keep estimates relative, and insist on clear acceptance criteria for high-priority items. Takeaway: a DEEP Product Backlog enables fast, confident planning and keeps stakeholders aligned on priorities.

keyIdea.title: DEEP
keyIdea.text: A healthy Product Backlog is Detailed appropriately, Estimated, Emergent, and Prioritized to enable effective planning.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › DEEP

Product Backlog: DEEP qualities

DEEP ensures backlog items are ready when needed and that the backlog remains a useful planning tool rather than a backlog of confusion.

Detailed appropriately
Top items have clear acceptance criteria and stakeholder intent; low-priority items remain high-level until they near delivery.
Estimated
Relative estimates let the Product Owner and team forecast capacity and prioritize by value per cost.
Emergent
The backlog evolves with new information, feedback, and changing context.
Prioritized
Ordering by value, risk, and necessity ensures the most important work is tackled first.
Concrete example
For a food-ordering app a top Product Backlog item such as "view menus" should include what screens are needed, performance expectations, and basic acceptance criteria. A distant idea like "loyalty program" can remain a headline with no immediate estimate.
Common Mistake
Skipping regular refinement leads to unclear stories and stalls during Sprint Planning.
Key Takeaway

Keep the backlog DEEP so high-priority work is ready, reducing planning friction and improving delivery predictability.

screens.title: Backlog Refinement: who, when, and how
screens.subtitle: Maintain readiness without overrunning team capacity

narration.text: Backlog refinement is the ongoing activity of adding detail, estimates, and ordering items in the Product Backlog. It is a collaborative activity led by the Product Owner, with active participation from the Development Team and stakeholders when needed. The goal is to make the top backlog items ready for upcoming Sprint Planning, but refinement should not consume more than a small portion of the Development Team's capacity — commonly suggested as about 10%, though teams may tailor this. Practical steps include clarifying acceptance criteria, splitting large epics into smaller stories, assigning relative estimates, and reordering by value and risk. A useful process is to run short, timeboxed refinement sessions each week and use just-in-time conversations for urgent clarifications. A frequent misconception is that refinement is a one-off event or solely the Product Owner's job; in fact, it is a shared, continuous practice that prevents planning bottlenecks and reduces wasted effort. Concrete example: before a Sprint that will deliver device control for a smart home hub, the team refines stories for secure login, device registration, and turn-on/off flows, ensuring each top story has clear acceptance criteria and a realistic estimate. Key takeaway: treat refinement as a collaborative habit that keeps the backlog healthy and planning fast.

keyIdea.title: Refinement practice
keyIdea.text: Refinement is a collaborative, ongoing activity that prepares high-priority backlog items for efficient Sprint Planning.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Refinement

Backlog Refinement: Process

A lightweight, regular habit to keep top backlog items ready without blocking delivery.

Step 1 — Clarify
Agree on acceptance criteria and the expected user outcome for the story.
Step 2 — Split
Break large epics into smaller, independently testable stories.
Step 3 — Estimate
Assign relative effort to enable forecasting during Sprint Planning.
Step 4 — Prioritize
Order by value, risk, and dependencies so the team builds the most important things first.
Practical guidance
Keep sessions short and focused. Reserve a small portion of capacity for refinement activities so they don't consume delivery time.
Misconception
Refinement is not a one-person job nor a single meeting; it is continuous and collaborative.
Key Takeaway

Timebox and share refinement so the backlog remains actionable and Sprint Planning stays efficient.

screens.title: Sprint Backlog: team-owned plan
screens.subtitle: What it contains and how it supports the Sprint Goal

narration.text: The Sprint Backlog is the Development Team’s plan for delivering the selected Product Backlog items and achieving the Sprint Goal. It contains the chosen Product Backlog items for the Sprint plus the tasks and design work needed to deliver them. Crucially, ownership of the Sprint Backlog belongs to the Development Team — they decide how to organize and execute the work. The Sprint Backlog is a highly visible, real-time picture of progress; as the team learns, they inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog accordingly. A common error is treating the Sprint Backlog as a rigid contract that cannot change after Sprint Planning. That misconception undermines the purpose of inspection and adaptation. Instead, the Sprint Goal should remain stable while the Sprint Backlog evolves to reflect new insights, impediments, or better approaches to achieving the goal. For example, if the team discovers an unforeseen integration challenge while building the menu display, they might re-sequence tasks or split a story into smaller tasks in the Sprint Backlog, always keeping the Sprint Goal in sight. Takeaway: the Sprint Backlog is the team's living plan to reach the Sprint Goal, and its adaptability is a feature, not a bug.

keyIdea.title: Sprint Backlog
keyIdea.text: A Development Team–owned, adaptable plan of selected backlog items and the work needed to reach the Sprint Goal.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Sprint Backlog

Sprint Backlog — team-owned plan

Contains selected Product Backlog items plus the plan for delivering them and achieving the Sprint Goal.

Contents
Selected items, tasks, design notes, and a forecast of work needed to reach the Sprint Goal.
Ownership
Owned solely by the Development Team — they set the plan and updates as they learn.
Adaptation
Updated continuously to reflect current understanding while keeping the Sprint Goal stable.
Concrete scenario
During a Sprint to build add-to-cart, the team adds tasks for UI, API, and unit tests to the Sprint Backlog and rearranges them when an API dependency appears.
Misconception
Viewing the Sprint Backlog as an inflexible contract removes the team’s ability to adapt to real discoveries.
Key Takeaway

The Sprint Backlog is a living plan the Development Team uses to inspect progress and adapt toward the Sprint Goal.

screens.title: Product Backlog vs Sprint Backlog
screens.subtitle: Ownership, lifespan, granularity, and evolution contrasted

narration.text: Understanding the difference between the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog is essential because it clarifies roles and expectations during planning and execution. The Product Backlog is owned by the Product Owner and is a dynamic, long-lived list of potential work that evolves over the product's lifecycle. It can contain high-level epics as well as more detailed user stories near the top. The Sprint Backlog, in contrast, is owned by the Development Team and exists only for the duration of a Sprint as a forecast and plan. Granularity differs: items in the Sprint Backlog are broken down into actionable tasks, while the Product Backlog may contain larger, less detailed items. Regarding evolution, Product Backlog items are continuously refined; Sprint Backlog items are adapted during the Sprint as the team learns, but the Sprint Goal should stay consistent. A common mistake is confusing ownership and expecting the Product Owner to manage daily task updates or expecting the Development Team to change the Product Backlog's long-term ordering. For example, the Product Owner may reorder features across releases based on stakeholder feedback, while the Development Team reprioritizes tasks within the Sprint Backlog to reach the Sprint Goal. Takeaway: keep responsibilities separate — Product Owner steers the backlog’s content and order; Development Team owns the Sprint plan.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Product Backlog is long-term, Product Owner–owned and emergent; Sprint Backlog is short-term, Development Team–owned and adaptable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Comparison

Product Backlog vs Sprint Backlog

Compare ownership, lifespan, granularity, and how each evolves to make practical distinctions clear.

Ownership
Product Backlog: Product Owner. Sprint Backlog: Development Team.
Lifespan
Product Backlog: ongoing across product. Sprint Backlog: lives for one Sprint as a plan.
Granularity
Product Backlog: mixed detail. Sprint Backlog: task-level detail for execution.
Evolution
Product Backlog: emergent and reordered by value. Sprint Backlog: adapted by team as learning occurs within Sprint.
Practical example
For a two-week Sprint to enable basic smart device control, the Product Backlog lists many features; the Development Team pulls specific stories like "register light bulb" and breaks them into tasks in the Sprint Backlog to meet the Sprint Goal.
Common Mistake
Expecting the Product Owner to manage daily task updates or letting the Sprint Backlog become a fixed contract removes team agility.
Key Takeaway

Respect different owners and cadences: one artifact guides product direction, the other guides short-term execution.

screens.title: Increment and Definition of Done
screens.subtitle: What 'Done' means and why it's non-negotiable

narration.text: An Increment is the sum of all Product Backlog items completed in a Sprint plus the value of all prior increments. For an Increment to be useful, it must meet the team's Definition of Done — a formal description of the state of the Increment that ensures quality measures are met. The Definition of Done often includes criteria such as code review, automated tests passing, integration, documentation updates, and security checks. Its purpose is to create transparency so everyone understands exactly what 'done' means. If an item does not meet the DoD, it cannot be considered part of the Increment, cannot be presented as Done in the Sprint Review, and should revert to the Product Backlog for future work. A common pitfall is an informal or weak DoD that allows 'almost done' work to accumulate, creating technical debt and hiding the true state of the product. For example, within a food-ordering app, a working menu display that has unit tests, has passed code review, and is deployed to staging meets the DoD; a menu that is partially tested or not integrated does not. Takeaway: DoD is a quality contract the Development Team uses to keep Increments genuine and releasable.

keyIdea.title: DoD importance
keyIdea.text: Definition of Done ensures Increments are genuinely releasable and prevents hidden technical debt caused by 'almost done' work.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Increment & DoD

Increment and Definition of Done

DoD defines the quality threshold an Increment must meet to be considered releasable and truly Done.

Increment
Sum of completed backlog items this Sprint plus previous Increments; must be usable regardless of release decision.
Definition of Done
A checklist of required quality practices that create a shared understanding of what Done means.
Enforcement
If an item doesn't meet DoD, it cannot be presented as Done and reverts to the Product Backlog.
Example: DoD checklist
  • • Code reviewed and merged
  • • Automated unit and integration tests passed
  • • Deployed to staging environment
  • • Security and performance sanity checks completed
Common Mistake
A vague DoD allows low-quality increments to hide behind the word "done."
Key Takeaway

Agree a practical, specific Definition of Done and apply it consistently so Increments are genuinely releasable.

screens.title: Using DoD in Sprint Review and Release
screens.subtitle: How DoD shapes what is shown, released, and kept on the backlog

narration.text: The Definition of Done plays a gatekeeping role during Sprint Review and release decisions. During Sprint Review, only backlog items that meet the DoD can be demonstrated as part of the Increment. This enforces transparency: stakeholders see real, usable progress rather than partially finished work. If a story fails DoD criteria during the Sprint, it returns to the Product Backlog for re-prioritization or continuation in a future Sprint. The Product Owner may choose whether to release an Increment, but release decisions are informed by the fact that the Increment meets the DoD and is therefore potentially releasable. A common misstep is to showcase incomplete work in reviews or to accept exceptions to the DoD to demonstrate progress; that undermines trust and accumulates hidden work. For instance, in the smart home hub scenario, if the add-to-cart equivalent — turning a light on — lacks automated tests or security checks required by DoD, the team should not list it as Done in the Sprint Review. Instead, document the shortfall, return it to the backlog, and adjust priorities. Takeaway: apply DoD consistently at review and release points to preserve transparency and reliability of increments.

keyIdea.title: DoD in review
keyIdea.text: DoD determines what can be shown or released; only items meeting DoD should be part of the Increment presented to stakeholders.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › DoD in Review

Applying DoD at Sprint Review

Only items that meet the Definition of Done should be presented as part of the Increment; otherwise they return to the backlog.

Show only Done work
This maintains stakeholder confidence and prevents "demo fudge" where incomplete work is misrepresented.
DoD informs release
The Product Owner may release when the Increment meets DoD and aligns with release goals.
If not Done
Revert the item to Product Backlog with clear next steps and re-estimate if needed.
Example
A tested menu display deployed to staging meets DoD and can be demoed. A partially integrated checkout cannot, and should not be marked Done in the review.
Pitfall
Allowing exceptions to DoD for demos hides real work and increases technical debt.
Key Takeaway

Be strict about DoD at review and release to keep product quality transparent and trustworthy.

screens.title: Example flow: Online food ordering
screens.subtitle: Trace a user story from Product Backlog to Done Increment

narration.text: Tracing a concrete example helps make artifacts meaningful. Consider building an online food ordering system. In the Product Backlog you might have items like "As a customer, I want to view restaurant menus" and "As a customer, I want to pay securely." The Product Owner orders these by value and risk. For an upcoming Sprint the team selects "Develop menu display page" and "Implement add-to-cart" into the Sprint Backlog, and the Development Team breaks these into tasks: UI markup, A P I endpoint, unit tests, and integration. During the Sprint the Development Team updates the Sprint Backlog as they discover a performance issue in the menu A P I and add a task to address caching. At the end of the Sprint the Increment contains the working, tested menu display — only if it meets the Definition of Done, including testing and deployment to staging. A misconception to avoid is presenting an unintegrated front-end as Done simply because the UI renders; integration and testing are DoD items. Key practical insight: moving an item through these artifacts clarifies what remains to be done and prevents surprises at review — and it gives stakeholders a reliable signal about usable progress.

keyIdea.title: Trace example
keyIdea.text: A user story becomes actionable when refined, planned into a Sprint Backlog, executed, and validated against the Definition of Done to become an Increment.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Applied Example

From backlog to Increment: menu display

Follow a user story as it moves from the Product Backlog into a Sprint Backlog and finally into a Done Increment.

Product Backlog
Item: "view restaurant menus" — prioritized and given acceptance criteria and an estimate.
Sprint Backlog
Selected stories plus tasks: UI markup, API endpoint, tests, deployment tasks owned by the Development Team.
Increment
Working menu display in staging that meets the Definition of Done and is potentially releasable.
Discovery example
If the team sees API performance problems while implementing the menu, they add and re-sequence work in the Sprint Backlog to address the issue and still focus on the Sprint Goal.
Misconception
A rendered UI alone is not Done unless integration and quality gates in the DoD are satisfied.
Key Takeaway

Trace items across artifacts to identify remaining work and make review conversations concrete and trustworthy.

screens.title: Hands-on: Smart Home Hub — select and plan
screens.subtitle: Transform Product Backlog items into a Sprint Backlog for a 2-week Sprint

narration.text: This hands-on activity practices selecting Product Backlog items for a Sprint and breaking them into tasks. The Sprint Goal is: enable users to securely connect and control basic smart devices. Given the prioritized items and a team capacity of about 15 to 20 story points, pick items that align to the Sprint Goal and fit capacity. For each selected item, break it into 2–3 actionable tasks such as UI, A P I, tests, or deployment steps. This exercise demonstrates how to balance value and effort, and how refinement creates ready-to-execute work. A common mistake is overcommitting by selecting too many large items; instead split large stories and prefer items with clear acceptance criteria. For example, selecting "register a new smart light bulb (8 points)" could yield tasks: implement device registration A P I, create registration UI, and write integration tests. Selecting the smaller "turn a registered light bulb on/off (3 points)" could yield tasks: implement control A P I and write unit tests. After selection, total the points and ensure they do not exceed team capacity. Takeaway: realistic selection and task breakdown create a workable Sprint Backlog and increase the chance of delivering a Done Increment.

keyIdea.title: Activity focus
keyIdea.text: Select backlog items aligned to the Sprint Goal and break them into specific tasks so the team can deliver a Done Increment within capacity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Hands-on

Sprint Goal

Enable users to securely connect and control basic smart devices (lights, thermostats).

Selected items (example)
• Register a new smart light bulb (8 points) • Turn a registered light on/off (3 points) • Secure login (5 points) — total 16 points, within a 15–20 point capacity.
Task breakdown example
Register light bulb tasks: API for device registration; UI for pairing; integration tests. Turn on/off tasks: control API; unit tests.
Template
Sprint Goal: Enable users to securely connect and control basic smart devices (lights, thermostats).

Item: Register a new smart light bulb (Estimate: 8)
  - Task 1.1: Implement device registration API
  - Task 1.2: Build pairing UI flow
  - Task 1.3: Write integration tests for registration

Item: Turn a registered light bulb on/off (Estimate: 3)
  - Task 2.1: Implement control API
  - Task 2.2: Write unit tests for control
Pitfall
Selecting unrefined, high-uncertainty items inflates risk and reduces likelihood of a Done Increment.
Key Takeaway

Choose items that align to the Sprint Goal and break them into clear tasks so the team can forecast and deliver reliably.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Practical fixes for stale backlogs, weak DoD, and rigid plans

narration.text: Teams commonly stumble in a few predictable ways when managing artifacts. First, the Product Backlog becomes stale when refinement stops; items lack detail and acceptance criteria, turning planning into a lengthy guessing game. Fix: timebox recurring refinement and make it collaborative so items near the top are always ready. Second, a weak Definition of Done lets partial work appear Done, hiding technical debt. Fix: define explicit, testable DoD items — for example, code review, passing tests, security checks, and deployment to staging — and apply them consistently. Third, treating the Sprint Backlog as a fixed contract removes the team’s ability to learn and adapt during the Sprint. Fix: keep the Sprint Goal stable but adapt tasks and sequencing to new discoveries. Fourth, ownership confusion leads to unclear decisions. Fix: Product Owner manages backlog content and order; Development Team owns the Sprint Backlog and execution. A practical tip: after each Sprint Review, update the Product Backlog using feedback, then schedule a short refinement session to ensure top items are ready. Takeaway: enforce simple discipline around refinement, DoD, and ownership to keep your artifacts honest and your delivery predictable.

keyIdea.title: Avoid errors
keyIdea.text: Prevent stalls and hidden debt by keeping backlog items refined, enforcing a strong Definition of Done, and preserving team-owned Sprint Backlogs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Common mistakes

Avoid these mistakes

Simple, repeatable fixes keep artifacts useful and accurate.

Stale Product Backlog
Fix: schedule short, regular refinement sessions and involve the Development Team.
Weak Definition of Done
Fix: agree specific, testable DoD items and apply them strictly at review and release.
Rigid Sprint Backlog
Fix: treat the Sprint Backlog as a forecast and adapt tasks as learning occurs while keeping the Sprint Goal intact.
Ownership confusion
Fix: Product Owner manages backlog content; Development Team manages Sprint Backlog and execution.
Practical tip
After Sprint Review, immediately capture feedback as backlog items and schedule a short refinement to prepare the top items for the next Sprint.
Key Takeaway

Discipline in refinement, DoD, and ownership prevents hidden rework and keeps delivery predictable.

screens.title: Assessment: applying the Definition of Done
screens.subtitle: Diagnose whether a feature is part of the 'Done' Increment

narration.text: Use assessment questions to check understanding of artifacts and DoD. Consider this scenario: a Development Team has completed coding and initial testing for a feature, but it has not been integrated into the main codebase and has not passed the team's security review, both of which are specified in their Definition of Done. Can this feature be presented as Done at the Sprint Review? The correct position is no, because it does not meet the full DoD and therefore isn't a truly releasable Increment. This reinforces the core claim that DoD is a quality contract and cannot be selectively applied to make a demo look better. A common misconception is to assume partial test completion or working UI is sufficient. To evaluate answers, ask learners to cite which DoD items are missing and propose how to move the work back to Done: integrate, complete security checks, and re-run automated tests, then validate against DoD before presenting. Practice diagnosing several scenarios and require learners to list missing DoD elements and the next backlog action. Takeaway: the DoD is binary for inclusion in an Increment — either met or not met — and that clarity preserves transparency.

keyIdea.title: Assessment focus
keyIdea.text: DoD is a binary quality gate: unless all DoD criteria are satisfied, work cannot be claimed as Done in the Increment.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Assessment

Assessment scenario

Decide whether partially finished work can be presented as Done according to the team's Definition of Done.

Scenario
Coding and initial testing are complete, but integration and security review required by DoD are not done.
Correct response: Not Done. Missing DoD items must be completed before the Increment can include this feature.
How to grade
Learners should list missing DoD items, explain why each matters, and describe the next steps to move the item back to Done.
Example checklist
Definition of Done (example):
• Code review completed
• Unit and integration tests passing
• Integrated into main branch
• Deployed to staging
• Security review completed
Key Takeaway

Use scenarios to practice identifying missing DoD items and the required remediation steps before accepting work as Done.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: These three concise concepts capture the chapter's essential classroom takeaways. First, the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's single source of product requirements and must be DEEP — detailed, estimated, emergent, and prioritized — so work is ready when needed. Second, the Sprint Backlog is the Development Team’s living plan for achieving the Sprint Goal; it is adaptable and contains the tasks that turn selected backlog items into a Done Increment. Third, the Increment must meet a clear Definition of Done; without a strong DoD, teams risk accumulating technical debt and misrepresenting progress. Keep these concepts visible in your team routines: refine the backlog regularly, let the team own and adapt the Sprint Backlog, and enforce DoD consistently. One final reflective question: which small change will you make this Sprint to improve transparency?

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: DEEP Product Backlog, team-owned adaptable Sprint Backlog, and a strict Definition of Done create reliable transparency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts
Product Backlog
An ordered, emergent list owned by the Product Owner; keep it DEEP.
Sprint Backlog
Development Team–owned plan of selected items and tasks, adapted during the Sprint.
Increment & DoD
Increments must meet a strict Definition of Done to be considered releasable and transparent.
Summary

Keep backlogs current, let the team own and adapt Sprint plans, and enforce DoD so progress remains visible and trustworthy.

narration.text: Keep these short definitions handy as a quick reference. Product Backlog: the Product Owner’s ordered, continuous list of potential work that should be DEEP. Sprint Backlog: the Development Team’s current Sprint plan that contains selected items and tasks and is adapted during the Sprint as new information arises. Increment: the sum of Done Product Backlog items that meet the Definition of Done and are potentially releasable. These three definitions form the backbone of Scrum’s transparency and inspection practices. When in doubt during planning or review, ask: does this item belong in the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog, or the Increment, and does it meet the Definition of Done? That quick check keeps conversations productive and aligned. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means short, memorable definitions for product backlog, sprint backlog, and increment to guide daily decisions.. In practical terms, three short definitions to memorize. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pocket definitions
keyIdea.text: Short, memorable definitions for Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment to guide daily decisions.

content.html:

Product Backlog
Ordered list of potential product work; DEEP ensures readiness and value focus.
Sprint Backlog
Team-owned plan for the Sprint; contains selected items and tasks and evolves with learning.
Increment
All Done backlog items that meet the Definition of Done; always potentially releasable.
Final takeaway

Use these pocket definitions as decision filters during refinement, planning, review, and release conversations.
